content.text: The Risks of Computing to Personal Safety and Identity

Topic 5.6 is the largest topic in Unit 5 and one of the most practically important. Computing innovations have created enormous benefits — but they have also created new risks to personal safety, privacy, and identity. This topic covers three areas: the privacy risks of personal data collection, how to protect computing resources through authentication and encryption, and how unauthorized access is gained through attacks like phishing, malware, and rogue access points.
Personally Identifiable Information (PII)

content.definition: Information about an individual that identifies, links, relates, or describes them. Examples: Social Security number, phone number, medical information, biometric data. Can be used for identity theft, stalking, or other criminal acts. Once placed online it is difficult to delete.

content.text: PII is any information that can be used to identify a specific individual. The key word is 'links' — PII does not have to directly name someone. A combination of data points that together identify a person is also PII. Social Security numbers, phone numbers, medical information, biometric data (fingerprints, facial recognition), and financial information are all examples of PII.
How PII Is Collected Online

content.definition: Search engines record search history. Websites record browsing history. Devices collect location data. Programs can record where you have been, how you got there, and how long you were there.

content.text: PII and other personal data are collected constantly during normal use of computing devices and the Internet. Most of this collection happens automatically and invisibly — users often do not know what is being collected, by whom, or for what purpose.

rows: Search engines
Every search query you type, when you typed it, and what results you clicked
Automatically logged with each search — linked to your account or device
Websites
Which pages you visit, how long you stay, what you click on
Tracking cookies stored on your device follow you across websites
Devices
Your physical location — where you are, where you have been, how you got there, how long you stayed
GPS, cell tower triangulation, Wi-Fi location services
Apps
Contacts, camera, microphone, location, and other device data — depending on permissions granted
Accessed through permissions you grant when installing the app
Social media platforms
Who you interact with, what content you view, what you post, how long you spend on each item
Tracked through the platform's own systems

content.text: Data Aggregation: When Pieces Combine

content.definition: Disparate personal data such as geolocation, cookies, and browsing history can be combined to create detailed knowledge about an individual. Combining information posted on social media with other sources can be used to deduce private information.

content.text: One of the most important privacy concepts in 5.6 is data aggregation. Individual pieces of data may seem harmless in isolation — your general location, your age range, your browsing interests. But when disparate data points are combined, they can create an extremely detailed profile of an individual that reveals information the person never intended to share.

rows: You searched for 'symptoms of depression'
+ your name and address from another source
Your private mental health struggles — shared with employers or insurers
You visited a fertility clinic's website
+ your location data showing you were in the clinic
+ your insurance ID from a data breach → insurance company knows you are trying to conceive
You posted photos from a vacation
+ your home city from your profile + timestamps of posts
You were away from home for 10 days — potential burglars know your house was empty
Your browsing history includes political news sites
+ your social media follows + your ZIP code
Your political leanings — used for targeted political advertising or voter profiling

content.label: Common Mistake
content.text: Students sometimes think that sharing individual pieces of information that seem harmless is safe. Data aggregation shows this is NOT true. Combining seemingly harmless pieces of data — geolocation, browsing history, social media posts, cookies — can reveal private information you never intended to share. The whole is much more revealing than the sum of its parts.
Benefits and Risks of PII Online

content.term: What are the benefits and risks of PII being online?
content.definition:
Benefits: enhances online experience, simplifies purchases, enables personalized suggestions.
Risks: can be used for identity theft, stalking, or criminal acts. Once online it is difficult to delete. Can be used in unintended and harmful ways.

rows: Personalized recommendations — streaming services suggest content you will like
Identity theft — SSN and financial info used to open fraudulent accounts
Simplified online shopping — saved payment and shipping info speeds checkout
Stalking — location data and personal info enable tracking of an individual's movements
Relevant search results — search history enables more useful suggestions
Criminal planning — PII can be used to target individuals for fraud, theft, or other crimes
Targeted advertising — businesses can reach genuinely interested customers
Unintended harmful use — information posted for one purpose used in ways never intended
Faster login and authentication — remembered accounts save time
Permanent record — once information is placed online it is difficult to delete

content.term: What can commercial and governmental entities do with collected data?
content.definition: Commercial and governmental curation of information may be exploited if privacy and other protections are ignored. Search engines can use search history for targeted marketing. Technology enables the exploitation of information about individuals.

Information placed online can be used in ways that were not intended and that may have a harmful impact. Once information is placed online it is difficult to delete. PII can be used for identity theft, stalking, or other criminal acts.
Users can control the permissions programs have for collecting user information. Users should review the permission settings of programs to protect their privacy.

content.text: Authentication: Protecting Access

content.definition: Measures that protect devices and information from unauthorized access. Examples: strong passwords and multifactor authentication. A strong password is easy for the user to remember but difficult for someone else to guess.

A method of access control where a user must present evidence from at least two of three categories: knowledge (something they know), possession (something they have), and inherence (something they are). Each step adds a new layer of security that must be broken to gain unauthorized access.

content.text: A strong password is something that is easy for a user to remember but would be difficult for someone else to guess based on knowledge of that user. This means a strong password avoids obvious personal information — birth dates, names, pet names, favorite sports teams — that someone who knows you could guess. Multifactor authentication adds additional layers on top of a password, making unauthorized access dramatically harder.

rows: Knowledge — something you KNOW
Information only the user should know
Password, PIN, security question answer, passphrase
Possession — something you HAVE
A physical device or token the user possesses
Phone that receives a text code, hardware security key, authenticator app, smart card
Inherence — something you ARE
A biometric characteristic unique to the user
Fingerprint scan, facial recognition, iris scan, voice recognition

content.code:
-- Multifactor authentication example:
-- Step 1 (Knowledge): Enter your password
--   → Password correct ✓
-- Step 2 (Possession): Enter the 6-digit code sent to your phone
--   → Code correct ✓
-- Access granted ✓

-- An attacker who steals your password STILL cannot access
-- your account without also having your phone
-- Each step adds a layer that must be independently broken

-- Single factor (password only):
-- Attacker steals password → immediate full access ✗

-- Two-factor (password + phone code):
-- Attacker steals password → still blocked without phone ✓

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: Know the three categories of multifactor authentication: knowledge (something you know), possession (something you have), and inherence (something you are). Multifactor means AT LEAST TWO of these categories — not just two steps of the same type. Using a password + a PIN is two knowledge factors — not multifactor. Using a password + a phone code IS multifactor (knowledge + possession).
Encryption: Protecting Data

content.definition: The process of encoding data to prevent unauthorized access. Decryption is the process of decoding the data. Two common approaches: symmetric key encryption (one key for both encryption and decryption) and public key encryption (public key to encrypt, private key to decrypt).

content.term: Symmetric Key vs Public Key Encryption
content.definition:
Symmetric key: uses one key for both encryption and decryption. Both sender and receiver must have the same key.
Public key: uses a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt. The sender does not need the receiver's private key to encrypt — only the receiver's private key can decrypt the message.

rows: Number of keys
ONE key — used for both encryption and decryption
TWO keys — a public key and a private key (a key pair)
Who has the key?
Both sender and receiver must have the SAME secret key
Public key is shared openly with anyone. Private key is kept secret by the receiver only.
How encryption works
Sender uses the shared key to encrypt. Receiver uses the same key to decrypt.
Sender uses receiver's PUBLIC key to encrypt. Only receiver's PRIVATE key can decrypt.
Key exchange challenge
How do sender and receiver securely share the key in the first place?
No challenge — public key can be shared openly with no security risk
Common use
Encrypting data at rest (stored files)
Secure internet communications (HTTPS websites)

content.text: The key insight about public key encryption is that the sender does not need the receiver's private key to send an encrypted message. The sender only needs the receiver's PUBLIC key — which can be shared openly without security risk. Only the receiver's PRIVATE key can decrypt the message. This solves the key exchange problem of symmetric encryption: you never have to securely share a secret key with the other party.

content.definition: Issues digital certificates that validate the ownership of encryption keys used in secure communications. Based on a trust model.

content.text: Certificate authorities solve a critical problem with public key encryption: how do you know that a public key actually belongs to who it claims to? A certificate authority is a trusted third party that issues digital certificates confirming that a public key genuinely belongs to the entity claiming to own it. When you visit a secure website (https://), a certificate authority has verified that the website's public key is legitimate.

content.label: Key Idea
content.text: Specific mathematical procedures for encryption and decryption are BEYOND THE SCOPE of this course and the AP exam. You need to understand: what encryption does (encodes data to prevent unauthorized access), the two approaches (symmetric vs public key), and the key difference (symmetric uses one key for both; public key uses public key to encrypt and private key to decrypt). You do NOT need to know the mathematical algorithms.
Malware and Computer Viruses

content.definition:
Malware: any software intended to damage a system or take partial control over it.
Computer virus: a specific type of malware that copies itself and attaches to legitimate programs. All viruses are malware but not all malware are viruses.
A malicious program that can copy itself and gain access to a computer in an unauthorized way. Viruses often attach themselves to legitimate programs and start running independently.

Software intended to damage a computing system or to take partial control over its operation. Untrustworthy downloads from freeware or shareware sites can contain malware. Computer virus and malware scanning software can help protect against infection.

rows: Malware (broad category)
Any software intended to damage a system or take partial control over it
Intent to cause harm — the defining feature
Ransomware, spyware, adware, trojans, worms, viruses
Computer virus (specific type)
Malicious program that copies itself and attaches to legitimate programs
Self-replication and attachment to legitimate programs — spreads itself
A virus that attaches to a word processor and spreads to every document you open
Ransomware
Malware that encrypts your files and demands payment to decrypt them
Holds data hostage for financial gain
Encrypts all files on your computer — demands Bitcoin payment
Spyware
Malware that secretly monitors your activity and sends data to attackers
Silent surveillance — you don't know it's there
Records your keystrokes, screenshots, and browsing history
Trojan
Malware disguised as legitimate software
Disguise — appears to be something useful
A free game download that secretly installs malware

content.term: Why are software updates important for security?
content.definition: All real-world systems have errors or design flaws that can be exploited. Regular software updates help fix these errors before attackers can use them.

content.text: How Unauthorized Access Is Gained

content.definition: A technique that attempts to trick a user into providing personal information. That information can then be used to access sensitive online resources such as bank accounts and emails. Can come through malicious links in emails or web pages.
The use of a program to record every keystroke made by a computer user in order to gain fraudulent access to passwords and other confidential information.
A wireless access point that gives unauthorized access to secure networks. Data sent over public networks can be intercepted, analyzed, and modified through a rogue access point.

content.term: How can emails be used to compromise security?
content.definition: Unsolicited emails, attachments, links, and forms can be used to compromise the security of a computing system. These can come from unknown senders or from known senders whose security has been compromised. A malicious link can be disguised on a web page or in an email.

rows: Phishing
Attacker sends a convincing fake email or website asking you to enter personal information — credentials go directly to the attacker
Never click links in unsolicited emails; go directly to websites by typing the URL; verify before entering any personal information
Keylogging
Malware secretly records every key you press — including passwords, credit card numbers, and messages — and sends the log to the attacker
Use malware scanning software; keep software updated; avoid downloading untrustworthy software
Rogue access point
Attacker sets up a fake Wi-Fi hotspot — when you connect, all your data flows through the attacker's device where it can be intercepted, read, and modified
Avoid using public Wi-Fi for sensitive activities; verify network authenticity; use VPN on public networks
Malicious email attachments
Attacker sends an email with a malicious file attached — opening it installs malware on your system
Never open attachments from unknown senders; be cautious even with known senders whose accounts may be compromised
Free/freeware downloads
Untrustworthy free software downloads contain hidden malware that installs alongside or instead of the advertised program
Download software only from trusted sources; use malware scanning software on all downloads

content.text: How to Protect Against Security Threats

content.term: How to protect against security threats
content.definition: Use strong passwords and multifactor authentication. Keep software updated regularly. Use virus and malware scanning software. Review app permission settings. Be cautious of unsolicited emails, attachments, links, and free downloads.

items: Use strong passwords — easy for you to remember, difficult for others to guess based on knowledge of you
Use multifactor authentication whenever available — adds a layer that must be independently broken
Keep software updated regularly — all real-world systems have errors that can be exploited; updates fix them
Use virus and malware scanning software — detects and removes malicious software
Review permission settings of programs — control what data apps can collect
Be cautious of unsolicited emails, attachments, and links — even from known senders whose accounts may be compromised
Avoid untrustworthy free downloads from freeware or shareware sites — these often contain malware
Be wary of public Wi-Fi — rogue access points can intercept your data

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: The AP exam tests all three attack types: phishing (tricks user into providing info), keylogging (records keystrokes to steal passwords), and rogue access point (fake Wi-Fi that intercepts data). Also know: malware is the broad category; virus is a specific type of malware that copies itself and attaches to legitimate programs. Software updates fix design flaws before attackers can exploit them.
